findings.description: publicly_accessible = true gives the RDS MySQL instance an internet-routable endpoint, exposing the database tier directly to untrusted networks and leaving only the security group as protection. The endpoint is also published as a Terraform output.
storage_encrypted = false explicitly disables RDS storage and snapshot encryption, so catalog data is written in cleartext and any actor with storage or snapshot access can read it.

The master password comes from var.password and the same value is interpolated into EC2 user_data, so the credential is persisted in Terraform state and in instance metadata instead of being retrieved from a secrets service; no IAM database authentication is enabled.

The user_data script embeds the RDS master username and password and writes them to /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc. EC2 user_data is retrievable in cleartext from the instance metadata service, so an SSRF in the hosted PHP app or any local foothold discloses the database master credentials.

The inline policy grants s3:*, ec2:* and rds:* on Resource "*" to the role assumed by the internet-facing web server. Compromise of the instance yields near-administrative control over all S3 data, EC2 (including role/instance manipulation for privilege escalation) and RDS in the account.

No metadata_options block enforcing IMDSv2 (http_tokens = "required") is set, so IMDSv1 remains enabled on a public-facing web server whose user_data holds DB credentials and whose instance profile carries wildcard permissions, creating a direct SSRF-to-credential-theft path.

MySQL port 3306 is opened to the entire VPC CIDR rather than only to the application instance's security group, so any workload in the VPC can reach the database directly, breaking least privilege and network segmentation.

The attached parameter group does not set require_secure_transport, so the MySQL instance accepts unencrypted connections, and the generated PHP client calls mysqli_connect with no TLS options, meaning credentials and query data can traverse the network in cleartext.

The egress rule permits all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0 from the database security group, giving a compromised database host an unconstrained outbound path for exfiltration or command-and-control callbacks.

No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so unless account-level default EBS encryption is enabled the root volume storing the plaintext dbinfo.inc credentials file is unencrypted at rest.

The master username is the well-known default "admin", which combined with the publicly reachable endpoint makes credential guessing and password spraying against the privileged account materially easier.
